member.name: T:N2.Core.Identity.Data.ApplicationSecret
member.summary: The secret store can contain secrets like a personal access token (PAT) to represents a token issued to an for authentication purposes. PATs are typically used for API access or other scenarios where a user needs to authenticate without using their primary credentials. But is may store other secrets too, like application secrets. The identifier is stored in a hashed form for security, and includes metadata such as name, expiration, and associated policies. The secret is linked to a specific entity and can be managed (created, revoked, listed) by the owner or administrators. For security, the actual token identifier is only shown at creation time and should not be retrievable afterwards. The hashed token is used for authentication purposes. The hash is generated using a secure algorithm (e.g., SHA-256) and uses the owners ID and MFA secret as part of the hashing process to ensure uniqueness and security. The expiration property allows for time-limited tokens, and the policies property can store JSON or other structured data defining the token's permissions and restrictions. The hash value is stored instead of the plain token to prevent misuse if the database is compromised. When a token is presented for authentication, it is hashed using the same algorithm and compared against the stored hash to verify its validity without ever exposing the original token value. The original token value should contain information for the owner identification and the algorithm used for hashing, so that the system can verify the token correctly.

member.summary: Registered automatically by EF Core design-time tooling. Replaces the default migration operation generator and snapshot annotation code generator with provider-agnostic equivalents, so that every generated migration — and its embedded Designer snapshot — works against both SQL Server and MySQL without post-editing.

member.name: T:N2.Core.Identity.Data.AgnosticMigrationOperationGenerator
member.summary:
Generates provider-agnostic migration code by:
Nullifying explicit column types so each provider resolves its own DDL type.
Adding a MySql:ValueGenerationStrategy annotation next to every SqlServer:Identity annotation so auto-increment columns work on both engines.
Removing SQL Server partial-index filter: expressions — MySQL UNIQUE indexes natively allow multiple NULLs, so no filter is required.

member.name: T:N2.Core.Identity.Data.AgnosticAnnotationCodeGenerator
member.summary:
Generates provider-agnostic snapshot and Designer-file code by omitting HasColumnType() from every property. This lets each provider resolve its own DDL type at migration-execution time (e.g. uniqueidentifier on SQL Server, char(36) on MySQL) instead of hard-coding a SQL Server type that MySQL cannot parse.
Index filters (HasFilter()) are intentionally kept: they are set unconditionally by ASP.NET Core Identity's OnModelCreating, so both the snapshot and the live model carry the annotation — the pending-model-changes check therefore sees no difference. The filter is stripped from the migration DDL at generation time by .

member.name: T:N2.Core.Identity.Services.ISecretManager
member.summary: Manages the full lifecycle of ApplicationSecret records.

para.b: Token vs. secret value — they are orthogonal

remarks.para:
The token and the secret value are two completely independent concepts:
Token (PlainToken)
A fixed-length authentication credential used to identify and look up a record. It contains owner identity and cryptographically random bytes, but carries no information about the secret value. Its length is constant for a given ownerType regardless of what is stored in ApplicationSecret.Secret. Knowing the token does not help an attacker recover the secret value.
Secret value (ApplicationSecret.Secret)
An arbitrary encrypted payload stored in the database. It is encrypted with AES-256-GCM and can only be decrypted by the implementation after successful token validation. Its size has no bearing on the token.

Every plaintext token produced by is a dot-separated string:
{base64url(ownerId)}.{ownerTypeCode}.{base64url(randomBytes)}
ownerIdBase64url-encoded bytes of the owner's . Note: the owner identifier is embedded in plaintext (base64url). Callers must never log, store in URLs, or expose tokens in contexts where the owner identity should remain private.
ownerTypeCodeAn 8-character base64url code derived from SHA-256(typeName)[0..5] via . Opaque — does not reveal the type name.
randomBytesCryptographically random bytes (minimum 32) that constitute the token's entropy. These have no relation to the stored secret value.
Embedding the owner identity in the token allows to resolve the correct owner record and its key material without any caller-supplied context. The full token string is HMAC-SHA256 signed with TokenSigningSecret and the result is stored in ApplicationSecret.HashedToken; the plaintext is never persisted. Using HMAC instead of a plain hash ensures that an attacker with read-only database access cannot pre-compute valid token hashes.

The secret value is encrypted with AES-256-GCM independently of the token. The key is derived via HKDF using:
IKMSystem secret (from configuration).
SaltPer-record random bytes in ApplicationSecret.EncryptionSalt.
InfoConcatenation of the owner's SecretKeyMaterial and HashedToken, binding the ciphertext to both this record and its owner.
A database dump alone is insufficient to recover the plaintext secret value.

member.name: M:N2.Core.Identity.Services.ISecretManager.ValidateAsync(System.String,System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary: Validates a plaintext token presented by a caller.

remarks.para:
The token must follow the format {base64url(ownerId)}.{ownerTypeCode}.{base64url(randomBytes)}. The implementation parses the owner identity from the token itself — no caller-supplied owner context is needed or accepted, eliminating the possibility of owner-confusion attacks. Steps performed:
Parse ownerId and ownerType from the token segments.
Look up the owner record to obtain its SecretKeyMaterial.
HMAC-SHA256 sign the full token with TokenSigningSecret and locate the ApplicationSecret by HashedToken.
Verify ReferenceId and ReferenceType match the parsed owner.
Check the record has not expired.
Derive the AES-256-GCM key via HKDF and decrypt ApplicationSecret.Secret.
Returns for unknown or expired tokens and on ownership mismatch — both without distinguishing the failure reason to avoid leaking token existence.

Callers are responsible for applying rate limiting and lockout policy before invoking this method. Implementations do not enforce per-IP or per-owner throttling internally. Repeated failed validation attempts should trigger back-off or revocation at the call site to prevent brute-force enumeration of token hashes.
